01-forces-and-motion.q: Which of these is a vector quantity?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: A vector has magnitude and direction. Velocity is speed in a stated direction; speed, distance and mass have size only.

01-forces-and-motion.q: Which of these is a scalar quantity?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Energy has no direction — it is a scalar. Force, acceleration and weight are all vectors.

01-forces-and-motion.q: A car travels 240 m in 30 s. What is its average speed?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: average speed = distance ÷ time = 240 ÷ 30 = 8 m/s.

01-forces-and-motion.q: A cyclist speeds up from 4 m/s to 10 m/s in 3 s. What is the acceleration?
What resultant force is needed to give a 1200 kg car an acceleration of 2.5 m/s²?
Taking g = 10 N/kg, what is the weight of a 65 kg student?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: W = m × g = 65 × 10 = 650 N. Weight is a force, measured in newtons.

01-forces-and-motion.q: In an exam answer, which term should you use for the downward force on a falling object?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Say weight or gravitational force. The examiners explicitly refuse bare 'gravity' — it appears in their reports every year.

01-forces-and-motion.q: A force of 50 N acts at a perpendicular distance of 40 cm from a pivot. What is the moment?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Convert first: 40 cm = 0.4 m. Moment = 50 × 0.4 = 20 N m. Answering 2000 means the cm were never converted — the classic lost mark.

01-forces-and-motion.q: What does the principle of moments say about a body in equilibrium?
options: All forces on it are zero
Clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments about a pivot
01-forces-and-motion.explain: For equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about a pivot equals the sum of anticlockwise moments.

01-forces-and-motion.q: A 2 N weight hangs 30 cm left of a pivot. Where must a 3 N weight hang to balance the rule?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: 2 × 30 = 60 N cm anticlockwise, so 3 × d = 60, d = 20 cm on the right.

01-forces-and-motion.q: What does Hooke's law state?
options: Extension is directly proportional to the force applied
Force is proportional to the square of extension
Extension is inversely proportional to force
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Extension is directly proportional to force, up to the limit of proportionality. The word 'directly' matters to the mark scheme.

01-forces-and-motion.q: A spring is stretched past its elastic limit. What happens when the force is removed?
options: It returns to its original length
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Beyond the elastic limit the deformation is plastic — the spring does not return to its original length.

01-forces-and-motion.q: On a distance–time graph, what does a horizontal line mean?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Flat distance–time = no distance being covered = stationary. (Flat velocity–time means constant velocity — don't mix the two.)

01-forces-and-motion.q: On a velocity–time graph, what does the area under the line give?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Area under a velocity–time graph is distance. The gradient gives acceleration.

01-forces-and-motion.q: On a velocity–time graph, what does the gradient give?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Gradient of velocity–time = change in velocity per second = acceleration.

01-forces-and-motion.q: What is thinking distance?
options: The distance travelled while the brakes are applied
The distance travelled during the driver's reaction time
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Thinking distance is covered during the driver's reaction time, before the brakes act. Braking distance is while the brakes are applied.

01-forces-and-motion.q: Which factor increases braking distance but NOT thinking distance?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Road conditions, brakes and mass affect braking distance only. Tiredness, alcohol and distraction affect the driver's reaction — thinking distance.

01-forces-and-motion.q: A car doubles its speed. What happens to its braking distance?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: From v² = u² + 2as, braking distance depends on speed squared — doubling speed quadruples it. Thinking distance only doubles.

01-forces-and-motion.q: A skydiver falls at terminal velocity. What is the resultant force on her?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: At terminal velocity air resistance equals weight, so the resultant force is zero and velocity is constant.

01-forces-and-motion.q: As a falling object speeds up, what happens to the air resistance acting on it?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Air resistance increases with speed. That is why the resultant force, and therefore the acceleration, decreases during the fall.

01-forces-and-motion.q: A ball is thrown straight up. Ignoring nothing, which forces act on it on the way UP?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Air resistance opposes motion. Going up, motion is upwards, so air resistance acts downwards — the same direction as weight.

01-forces-and-motion.q: A book rests on a table. The table pushes up on the book with a force equal to its weight. Why are these forces equal?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Both forces act on the same object (the book), so they cannot be a third-law pair. They are equal because the book is in equilibrium.

01-forces-and-motion.q: What is the third-law partner of the Earth pulling down on a book (the book's weight)?
options: The table pushing up on the book
The book pushing down on the table
The book pulling up on the Earth
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Third-law pairs act on different objects and are the same type of force: Earth pulls book, book pulls Earth.

01-forces-and-motion.q: A car brakes from 20 m/s to rest over 40 m. Using v² = u² + 2as, what is the deceleration?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: 0 = 20² + 2 × a × 40 → 400 = −80a → a = −5, a deceleration of 5 m/s².

01-forces-and-motion.q: You are given u, v and s but no time. Which equation should you reach for?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: No time given is the signal for v² = u² + 2as — it is the only motion equation without t in it.

01-forces-and-motion.q: What is the centre of gravity of an object?
options: The point where it balances on a finger
The point through which its whole weight acts
The heaviest part of the object
01-forces-and-motion.explain: The centre of gravity is the point through which the whole weight of the body acts — the accepted definition.

01-forces-and-motion.q: A uniform metre rule is pivoted at its centre. Why can its own weight be ignored in moment calculations?
options: Its weight acts at the pivot, so its perpendicular distance is zero
The rule pushes up on itself
01-forces-and-motion.explain: The rule's weight acts at its centre of gravity — the midpoint — which is at the pivot. Distance zero means moment zero.

01-forces-and-motion.q: Which phrase earns the mark: the falling object stops accelerating because…
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Say 'the resultant force is zero'. 'The forces are equal' is on the exact list of phrases the mark schemes refuse.

01-forces-and-motion.q: On a force–extension graph for a spring, what does the area under the line give?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Area under force–extension is the energy stored in the spring (the elastic store).

01-forces-and-motion.q: A velocity–time graph shows a straight line from 0 to 20 m/s in 8 s. What is the distance travelled?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Area under the line = ½ × 8 × 20 = 80 m (a triangle, since it starts from rest).

01-forces-and-motion.q: Which distance is measured from the moment the driver sees a hazard to the moment the brakes are applied?
options: Reaction distance is not a real quantity
01-forces-and-motion.explain: That interval is the reaction time; the distance covered in it is the thinking distance. Stopping distance = thinking + braking.

01-forces-and-motion.q: An 80 kg parachutist has weight 800 N and feels 500 N of air resistance. What is her acceleration?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Resultant force = 800 − 500 = 300 N. a = F ÷ m = 300 ÷ 80 = 3.75 m/s².

01-forces-and-motion.q: The gradient of a distance–time graph gives…
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Distance ÷ time = speed. Acceleration is the gradient of a VELOCITY–time graph; the area under a velocity–time graph is distance.

01-forces-and-motion.q: The area under a velocity–time graph gives…
01-forces-and-motion.explain: velocity × time = distance. The gradient of that same graph is acceleration — one of the commonest mix-ups in the reports.

01-forces-and-motion.q: A car travels at a constant 20 m/s for 8 s. The distance travelled is…
01-forces-and-motion.explain: distance = speed × time = 20 × 8 = 160 m. 2.5 is the upside-down division.

01-forces-and-motion.q: A 60 kg student stands on Earth (g = 10 N/kg). Their weight is…
01-forces-and-motion.explain: W = m × g = 60 × 10 = 600 N. Weight is a FORCE in newtons; 600 kg would be a mass. Mass never changes with location — weight does.

01-forces-and-motion.q: An object falls at terminal velocity. The resultant force on it is…
options: equal to the air resistance plus weight
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Terminal velocity means constant velocity, so the forces balance: weight = air resistance and the resultant is zero. No resultant force means no acceleration.

01-forces-and-motion.q: A resultant force of 12 N acts on a 4 kg mass. The acceleration is…
01-forces-and-motion.explain: a = F ÷ m = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 m/s². Rearranging F = ma is examined every year — write the formula first, then substitute.

01-forces-and-motion.q: The moment of a force is calculated as…
options: force × distance moved in the direction of the force
force × perpendicular distance from the pivot
01-forces-and-motion.explain: moment = F × perpendicular distance from the pivot, in N m. Force × distance moved is WORK — different quantity, different unit (J).

01-forces-and-motion.q: A spring obeys Hooke's law. This means extension is…
options: directly proportional to the force applied
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Directly proportional — a straight line through the origin on a force–extension graph, up to the limit of proportionality where it curves.

01-forces-and-motion.q: Which pair are both vector quantities?
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Vectors have magnitude AND direction: velocity, force, acceleration, weight, momentum. Speed, distance, mass, time and energy are scalars.

01-forces-and-motion.q: Stopping distance is made up of…
01-forces-and-motion.explain: Thinking distance (during reaction time) plus braking distance (while decelerating). Tiredness or alcohol raises thinking distance; wet roads or worn tyres raise braking distance.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: A block has mass 240 g and volume 30 cm³. What is its density?
Which equation links pressure, force and area?
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Pressure = force ÷ area. Same force on a smaller area gives a larger pressure.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: How are the particles arranged in a solid?
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Solids: regular arrangement, closely packed, vibrating about fixed positions.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: Which description of particle motion in a liquid earns the mark?
options: They fly around at high speed
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Liquid particles slide/flow/move past each other. Bare 'they move' scores nothing — an explicit examiner ruling.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: How are the particles arranged in a liquid?
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Liquids keep the close packing of solids but lose the regular arrangement — random/irregular but touching. Students regularly lose this mark by saying liquids spread out.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: Convert 27 °C to kelvin.
Convert 350 K to degrees Celsius.
What is absolute zero?
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Absolute zero is 0 K = −273 °C — the temperature at which particles have minimum kinetic energy.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: How does a gas exert pressure on its container?
options: Particles collide with the walls, each collision exerting a force
The gas pushes down due to gravity
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Randomly moving particles collide with the walls; each collision exerts a force, and pressure = force ÷ area. Name the particles — 'they hit the walls' scores nothing.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: A sealed gas is heated at constant volume. Why does the pressure rise?
options: Particles hit the walls harder and more often
The particles stick to the walls
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Higher temperature means greater average kinetic energy — particles hit the walls more often and with more force. The particles themselves do not expand.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: Which law links pressure and volume at constant temperature?
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Boyle's law: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ at constant temperature.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: A gas at 100 kPa in 3.0 m³ is compressed to 1.0 m³ at constant temperature. What is the new pressure?
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂: 100 × 3 = p₂ × 1, so p₂ = 300 kPa. Smaller volume, higher pressure.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: Using the pressure law, what must the temperature be measured in?
options: Either, as long as you are consistent
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: p ÷ T = constant only works with absolute temperature — kelvin. Using °C is a standard exam error.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: A gas has pressure 120 kPa at 300 K. It is heated to 360 K at constant volume. What is the new pressure?
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: p₁/T₁ = p₂/T₂: 120 ÷ 300 = p₂ ÷ 360 → p₂ = 144 kPa.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: Which equation gives the energy needed to change a substance's temperature?
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: ΔQ = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: How much energy raises the temperature of 0.5 kg of water (c = 4200 J/kg °C) by 20 °C?
A student uses 16 g of water in a specific heat capacity calculation. What must they do before substituting?
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: c is in J/kg °C, so mass must be in kg: 16 g = 0.016 kg. The examiners called g→kg the single most common cause of lost marks on this topic.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: What is specific heat capacity?
options: The energy to melt 1 kg of a substance
The energy to raise 1 kg by 1 °C
The maximum heat a substance can hold
The temperature at which a substance boils
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1 °C.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: Water has a higher specific heat capacity than oil. Equal masses receive equal energy. Which heats up more?
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Lower c means less energy needed per degree — the oil's temperature rises more for the same energy.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: During melting, what happens to the temperature of a substance?
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: During a change of state the energy goes into breaking bonds between particles, not raising temperature — the temperature–time graph is flat.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: What is the pressure difference 5 m deep in water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 N/kg)?
Why does pressure increase with depth in a liquid?
options: There is more weight of liquid above
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: The deeper you go, the greater the weight of liquid above pressing down.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: In the gas equations, what does a temperature increase do to average particle kinetic energy?
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Temperature (in kelvin) is directly proportional to average kinetic energy. Note: temperature is proportional to KE — temperature IS NOT kinetic energy.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: Which statement about temperature and kinetic energy earns the mark?
options: Temperature is directly proportional to average kinetic energy (in kelvin)
Kinetic energy is temperature times mass
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: The examiners specifically penalise 'temperature is kinetic energy'. It is directly proportional to the average KE, with temperature in kelvin.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: To find the volume of an irregular object, which method is standard?
options: Water displacement with a measuring cylinder or eureka can
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Submerge it fully and measure the displaced water — the displacement method. Detail marks: fully submerged, no splashing, read at eye level.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: A plastic bottle is sealed in a plane at altitude and crushed on landing. Why?
options: Air pressure outside becomes greater than inside
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Cabin pressure at altitude is lower; on descent the outside pressure rises above the pressure sealed inside, giving a resultant inward force.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: Which change of state releases energy?
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Condensing (gas → liquid) and freezing release energy as bonds form. Melting and evaporating absorb energy.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: 1 g/cm³ is the density of water. What is that in kg/m³?
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. Know this conversion — it is a common substitution trap.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: Why can gases be compressed but liquids essentially cannot?
options: Gas particles are far apart with space between them; liquid particles are already touching
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Compression reduces the space between particles. Gas particles have large gaps; liquid particles are already closely packed.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: In the SHC-of-a-block practical, why is the block lagged (insulated)?
options: To reduce energy transfer to the surroundings
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Lagging reduces energy loss to the surroundings, so more of the electrical energy goes into the block — the measured c is closer to the true value.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: In that practical, energy is lost to the surroundings anyway. How does this affect the calculated value of c?
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: You divide the (too large) electrical energy by the temperature rise, so the calculated c comes out higher than the true value.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: Boyle's law requires which quantity to stay constant?
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Boyle's law (p₁V₁ = p₂V₂) holds at constant temperature for a fixed mass of gas.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: The density of an object is calculated as…
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: ρ = m ÷ V, in kg/m³ or g/cm³. Using weight instead of mass is a classic slip — density uses MASS.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: Pressure is calculated as…
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: p = F ÷ A, in pascals (N/m²). The same force over a smaller area gives a bigger pressure — why a drawing pin works.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: The pressure due to a column of liquid is p = h × ρ × g. Doubling the DEPTH will…
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Pressure is directly proportional to depth. Note it does not depend on the width or shape of the container — only depth, density and g.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: In the kinetic theory, the particles of a gas…
options: are close together and vibrate in fixed positions
move randomly at high speed with large gaps between them
are close together but can slide past each other
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Gas: random, fast, far apart. Solid: vibrating in fixed positions. Liquid: close but sliding past each other.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: A temperature of 27 °C in kelvin is…
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: K = °C + 273, so 27 + 273 = 300 K. Every gas-law calculation must use kelvin — this conversion is where the marks go.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: Boyle's law (p₁V₁ = p₂V₂) applies when…
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Constant temperature (and fixed mass of gas). Squeeze the volume and the pressure rises in proportion.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: A gas is heated in a sealed rigid container. The pressure rises because the particles…
options: collide with the walls more often and harder
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: More kinetic energy → faster particles → more frequent, harder collisions with the walls. The particles themselves never change size, and the volume is fixed.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: The volume of a 0.5 kg block of density 2000 kg/m³ is…
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: V = m ÷ ρ = 0.5 ÷ 2000 = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m³. Rearranging the density formula, and keeping the tiny answer in standard form, is the tested skill.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: When a solid melts, the particles…
options: gain energy and the forces between them weaken enough to slide
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Energy in, arrangement loosens — they can move past each other. During melting the temperature stays constant because the energy goes into breaking the bonds, not raising the temperature.

02-solids-liquids-gases.q: Gas pressure inside a container is caused by…
options: particles colliding with the container walls
02-solids-liquids-gases.explain: Countless tiny collisions with the walls; each exerts a force, and force per unit area is pressure.

03-electrical-circuits.q: Which equation links voltage, current and resistance?
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Ohm's law: V = I × R.

03-electrical-circuits.q: A current of 0.25 A flows through a 48 Ω resistor. What is the voltage across it?
Which equation links charge, current and time?
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Charge = current × time. One amp is one coulomb per second.

03-electrical-circuits.q: A current of 0.4 A flows for 90 s. How much charge passes?
What is electric current?
options: The rate of flow of charge
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Current is the rate of flow of charge. In a metal it is a flow of negatively charged electrons.

03-electrical-circuits.q: What is voltage (potential difference)?
options: The rate of flow of charge
The energy transferred per unit charge
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Voltage is the energy transferred per unit charge passed — one volt is one joule per coulomb.

03-electrical-circuits.q: In a series circuit, what is true of the current?
options: It is the same at every point
It is zero at the battery
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Series: same current everywhere. It is the voltage that is shared between components.

03-electrical-circuits.q: In a parallel circuit, what is true of the voltage across each branch?
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Each parallel branch gets the full supply voltage; the current splits between branches.

03-electrical-circuits.q: Two resistors, 15 Ω and 10 Ω, are in series. What is the total resistance?
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Series resistances add: 15 + 10 = 25 Ω.

03-electrical-circuits.q: Adding a second resistor in parallel with a first. What happens to the total resistance?
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Parallel paths give the current more routes — total resistance is less than the smallest branch.

03-electrical-circuits.q: At a junction, 0.5 A flows in and one branch carries 0.2 A. What does the other branch carry?
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Current into a junction equals current out: 0.5 − 0.2 = 0.3 A.

03-electrical-circuits.q: How must an ammeter and voltmeter be connected to measure a lamp?
options: Ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel with the lamp
Ammeter in parallel, voltmeter in series
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Ammeter in series (current through it), voltmeter in parallel across the component (voltage across it). Every past paper asks for this circuit.

03-electrical-circuits.q: The I–V graph of a filament lamp curves, becoming less steep. Why?
options: The lamp runs out of electrons
The filament heats up and its resistance increases
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Current heats the filament; hotter metal ions vibrate more, causing more electron collisions — resistance rises, so current rises less per volt.

03-electrical-circuits.q: Which component only lets current flow one way?
03-electrical-circuits.explain: A diode conducts in one direction only — its I–V graph is flat (no current) in reverse.

03-electrical-circuits.q: What happens to an LDR's resistance as light intensity increases?
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Light-dependent resistor: brighter light, lower resistance. The relationship is a curve, not a straight line.

03-electrical-circuits.q: What happens to a thermistor's resistance as temperature increases?
03-electrical-circuits.explain: For the thermistors on this course, resistance falls as temperature rises.

03-electrical-circuits.q: Which equation links electrical power, current and voltage?
03-electrical-circuits.explain: P = I × V — power in watts, current in amps, voltage in volts.

03-electrical-circuits.q: A kettle draws 10 A at 230 V. What is its power?
Which equation gives the energy transferred by a charge moving through a potential difference?
03-electrical-circuits.explain: E = Q × V — energy (J) = charge (C) × voltage (V).

03-electrical-circuits.q: In a metal wire, what actually moves to make the current?
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Current in a metal is a flow of negatively charged electrons. The positive metal ions stay in place, vibrating.

03-electrical-circuits.q: Two identical resistors in series across a 6 V battery. What is the voltage across each?
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Series voltage is shared; identical resistors share it equally: 3 V each.

03-electrical-circuits.q: A 15 Ω and a 10 Ω resistor are in parallel across 3 V. What is the total current from the battery?
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Each branch gets 3 V: I = 3/15 + 3/10 = 0.2 + 0.3 = 0.5 A.

03-electrical-circuits.q: The same two resistors are reconnected in series across 3 V. What is the current now?
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Series: R = 25 Ω, I = 3 ÷ 25 = 0.12 A — much less than the 0.5 A in parallel. Comparison questions need this sentence, not just the numbers.

03-electrical-circuits.q: In exam circuit drawings, the most common lost marks are for…
options: Gaps in the circuit and wrong symbols
03-electrical-circuits.explain: The examiners repeatedly flag unclosed circuits and wrong symbols — a variable resistor drawn as a thermistor is their standard example.

03-electrical-circuits.q: Which symbol difference matters: a variable resistor vs a thermistor?
options: Variable resistor has an arrow through it; thermistor has a bent line through it
Variable resistor is drawn as a zigzag only
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Variable resistor: rectangle with a diagonal arrow. Thermistor: rectangle with a bent line. Swapping them costs the symbol mark.

03-electrical-circuits.q: A 6 V battery drives 0.05 A through a bulb for 60 s. How much energy is transferred? (E = I × V × t)
The I–V graph of a fixed resistor at constant temperature is…
options: A straight line through the origin
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Constant resistance means current is directly proportional to voltage — a straight line through the origin.

03-electrical-circuits.q: Why is a series circuit with one switch able to turn everything off?
options: Breaking the single loop stops current everywhere
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Series components share one loop — break it anywhere and the current stops everywhere.

03-electrical-circuits.q: Which quantity is measured in coulombs?
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Charge is measured in coulombs (C). Current is amps, voltage volts, resistance ohms.

03-electrical-circuits.q: A voltmeter should have a very high resistance. Why?
options: So almost no current flows through it, leaving the circuit unaffected
03-electrical-circuits.explain: A voltmeter sits in parallel; high resistance means it draws almost no current and doesn't disturb what it is measuring.

03-electrical-circuits.q: Two resistors in series: 19 Ω and 13 Ω across 2.9 V. What is the current?
03-electrical-circuits.explain: R = 19 + 13 = 32 Ω; I = 2.9 ÷ 32 ≈ 0.09 A — the exact calculation from the 2025 paper's Q5(b)(iv).

03-electrical-circuits.q: In a parallel circuit, the current from the battery equals…
options: The current in the smallest branch
The sum of the branch currents
03-electrical-circuits.explain: The branch currents recombine: total current = sum of the branches.

03-electrical-circuits.q: Current is measured with an ammeter connected…
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Ammeters go in series (the current must flow through them); voltmeters go in parallel (across the component).

03-electrical-circuits.q: In a series circuit, the current…
03-electrical-circuits.explain: One path, so the same current everywhere. It is the VOLTAGE that splits between components in series.

03-electrical-circuits.q: In a parallel circuit, each branch has…
options: a smaller voltage than the supply
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Each branch gets the full supply voltage; the current divides between branches. This is why house lights are wired in parallel.

03-electrical-circuits.q: A 12 V supply drives 3 A through a resistor. Its resistance is…
03-electrical-circuits.explain: R = V ÷ I = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 Ω. State the formula, then substitute — 'state the equation' is a free mark asked nearly every year.

03-electrical-circuits.q: The equation linking charge, current and time is…
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Q = I × t — charge in coulombs, current in amps, time in SECONDS. Converting minutes to seconds is where marks are lost.

03-electrical-circuits.q: Electrical power is calculated as…
03-electrical-circuits.explain: P = I × V in watts (also P = I²R). Energy transferred is E = I × V × t.

03-electrical-circuits.q: As the temperature of a thermistor increases, its resistance…
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Thermistor: hotter → lower resistance (used in temperature sensors). LDR: brighter → lower resistance. Both go DOWN with more of their stimulus.

03-electrical-circuits.q: A fuse protects a circuit by…
options: melting and breaking the circuit if the current is too high
03-electrical-circuits.explain: A deliberately weak link: too much current melts the wire and cuts the circuit. It should be rated just above the appliance's normal current.

03-electrical-circuits.q: The three wires in a UK mains cable are…
03-electrical-circuits.explain: Live (brown, 230 V), neutral (blue, ~0 V), earth (green/yellow, safety). The earth wire plus the fuse together protect a metal-cased appliance.

03-electrical-circuits.q: Two 4 Ω resistors in series have a total resistance of…
03-electrical-circuits.explain: In series resistances simply add: 4 + 4 = 8 Ω. In parallel the total is always LESS than the smallest single resistor (2 Ω here).

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: In a transverse wave, the vibrations are…
options: Parallel to the direction of energy transfer
Perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Transverse: vibrations perpendicular to the direction of travel. Light and all EM waves are transverse.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: In a longitudinal wave, the vibrations are…
options: Perpendicular to the direction of travel
Parallel to the direction of travel
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Longitudinal: vibrations parallel to the direction of energy transfer. Sound is the standard example.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: Which equation links wave speed, frequency and wavelength?
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Wave speed = frequency × wavelength.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: A sound wave travels at 340 m/s with frequency 425 Hz. What is its wavelength?
What is the frequency of a wave?
options: The number of complete waves passing a point per second
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Frequency = waves per second, measured in hertz. Both parts — 'complete waves' and 'per second' — carry marks.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: What is the amplitude of a wave?
options: The maximum displacement from the rest position
The full height from trough to crest
The length of the wave train
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Amplitude is measured from the rest (undisturbed) position to a crest — not trough to crest.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: 30 kHz written in hertz is…
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: kilo = ×1000, so 30 kHz = 30 000 Hz. Convert before substituting into v = fλ.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: Put these in order of increasing frequency:
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Radio → microwaves → infrared → visible → ultraviolet → X-rays → gamma, in increasing frequency.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: Which EM waves have the highest frequency?
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Gamma rays sit at the top of the spectrum — highest frequency, shortest wavelength.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: Which part of the EM spectrum sits immediately above visible light in frequency?
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Above visible: ultraviolet. Below visible: infrared.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: Which property do ALL electromagnetic waves share?
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: All EM waves are transverse, transfer energy, and travel at the same speed in a vacuum (3 × 10⁸ m/s).

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: Which is a correct use of microwaves?
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Microwaves: heating food, communications, radar. The 2025 examiners rejected 'microwaving food' — say heating.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: Which is an accepted use of gamma rays?
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Gamma: sterilising equipment or food, treating cancer, medical tracing. 'Curing cancer' and vague 'medicine' were rejected — be specific.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: What danger is associated with ultraviolet radiation?
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: UV causes skin cancer and eye damage. Each band's danger is asked with its use — learn them as pairs.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: A sound pulse returns from the seabed in 0.16 s. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in water. How deep is the sea?
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Total distance = 1500 × 0.16 = 240 m — but that is there AND back. Depth = 120 m. Forgetting the factor of 2 is the classic sonar error.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: Why can sound not travel through a vacuum?
options: There are no particles to vibrate
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Sound is a mechanical wave — it needs particles. Light, being electromagnetic, crosses a vacuum happily.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: Sound is which type of wave?
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Sound is longitudinal — the air particles vibrate parallel to the direction the sound travels.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: A source of sound moves towards you. What happens to the frequency you hear?
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Doppler effect: wavefronts ahead of a moving source are compressed — shorter wavelength, higher frequency.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: In the Doppler effect, what stays constant while wavelength and frequency change?
options: The wave speed in that medium
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: The speed depends on the medium, not the source. Compressed wavelength with constant speed forces the frequency up — that is the 3-mark chain.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: Light travels at 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. A wave has wavelength 5.4 × 10⁻⁷ m. What is its frequency?
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: f = v ÷ λ = 3.0 × 10⁸ ÷ 5.4 × 10⁻⁷ = 5.6 × 10¹⁴ Hz. The 2025 mark scheme accepted 5.6 but rejected 5.5 — sig figs matter.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: What is the time period of a wave with frequency 50 Hz?
Which difference between sound and light is correct?
options: Sound is transverse, light is longitudinal
Sound needs a medium, light does not
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Sound is longitudinal and needs a medium; light is transverse, electromagnetic, and much faster.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: What is a wavefront?
options: A line joining points on a wave that are in phase
The crest of the biggest wave
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: A wavefront joins all points in phase — like the crest lines of ripples.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: The wavelength of a wave is the distance between…
options: A crest and the next trough
A point on one wave and the same point on the next
The rest position and a crest
The start and end of vibration
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: One complete wave: same point to same point (crest to crest, or any point to its repeat).

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: Why can astronauts on the Moon not talk to each other directly without radios?
options: There is no air to carry sound
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: No atmosphere — no particles — no medium for sound. Radio (EM) waves cross the vacuum instead.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: Which wave property determines the loudness of a sound?
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Bigger amplitude, louder sound. Frequency determines pitch.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: Which wave property determines the pitch of a sound?
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Higher frequency = higher pitch. Amplitude controls loudness.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: X-rays are used in hospitals to…
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: X-rays penetrate soft tissue but are absorbed by bone — that contrast makes the image.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: Infrared radiation is used for…
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Infrared: heaters, thermal imaging, night vision, remote controls.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: A wave has period 0.005 s. What is its frequency?
Radio waves and gamma rays both…
options: Travel at the same speed in a vacuum
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: All EM waves share the vacuum speed of 3 × 10⁸ m/s — the spectrum differs in frequency and wavelength, not speed.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: As frequency increases across the EM spectrum, the wavelength…
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: v = fλ with constant v: frequency up means wavelength down. Gamma has the shortest wavelength.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: The equation linking wave speed, frequency and wavelength is…
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: v = f λ. Convert kHz and MHz to hertz before substituting — the reports flag this every year.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: A wave has frequency 40 kHz. In hertz that is…
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: kilo = ×1000, so 40 kHz = 40 000 Hz. A 2025 question hinged on exactly this conversion before using v = fλ.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: In a transverse wave, the vibrations are…
options: parallel to the direction of travel
perpendicular to the direction of travel
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Transverse: vibration at right angles to travel (light, water, all EM waves). Longitudinal: vibration along the direction of travel (sound).

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: Which lists the electromagnetic spectrum from LONGEST wavelength to shortest?
options: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma
Gamma, X-ray, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave, radio
Radio, infrared, microwave, visible, X-ray, ultraviolet, gamma
Visible, radio, microwave, infrared, gamma, X-ray, ultraviolet
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Radio → gamma is longest → shortest wavelength (and lowest → highest frequency). The order must be memorised; it is asked directly.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: Which EM wave is used for cooking and mobile phone signals?
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Microwaves. Infrared is used for remote controls, thermal imaging and grills; UV for security marking and sun-tanning; X-rays for imaging bones.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: The danger of ultraviolet radiation is that it…
options: damages surface cells and can cause skin cancer
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: UV: skin cancer and eye damage. Microwaves heat internal tissue; X-rays and gamma ionise and mutate cells; infrared burns the skin.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: When light passes from air into glass it slows down and bends…
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Into a denser medium: slower, bends TOWARDS the normal. Coming out into air it speeds up and bends away. The frequency never changes.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: The law of reflection states that…
options: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
the angle of incidence is twice the angle of reflection
the angles are measured from the mirror surface
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: i = r, and both are measured from the NORMAL (the perpendicular), never from the surface — a diagram-labelling mark.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: Ultrasound is sound with a frequency…
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: Above the human hearing range (20 Hz – 20 kHz). Used for pre-natal scanning and measuring distance from echo times.

04-waves-and-em-spectrum.q: A ship's sonar pulse returns after 0.4 s in water where sound travels 1500 m/s. The depth is…
04-waves-and-em-spectrum.explain: The pulse goes down AND back: total distance = 1500 × 0.4 = 600 m, so the depth is half that — 300 m. Forgetting to halve is the standard error.

05-static-electricity.q: A plastic rod is rubbed with a cloth and becomes negatively charged. What has happened?
options: Electrons moved from the cloth to the rod
Electrons moved from the rod to the cloth
05-static-electricity.explain: Only electrons move in static electricity. The rod gained electrons; the cloth is left positive. Any mention of protons moving is a knowledge error.

05-static-electricity.q: What charge is left on the cloth in that experiment?
05-static-electricity.explain: The cloth lost electrons, so it is left with an equal positive charge.

05-static-electricity.q: Which particles are transferred when objects are charged by friction?
05-static-electricity.explain: Electrons only. Protons are locked in the nucleus.

05-static-electricity.q: Two objects carry the same charge. What do they do?
05-static-electricity.explain: Like charges repel; opposite charges attract.

05-static-electricity.q: A charged rod attracts small pieces of paper even though the paper is uncharged. Why?
options: The rod induces opposite charge on the near side of the paper
05-static-electricity.explain: The rod's charge shifts electrons within the paper, leaving the near surface oppositely charged — so it attracts. Attraction of an uncharged insulator demonstrates charge.

05-static-electricity.q: Why does charge build up on plastic but not on an earthed metal?
options: Plastic is an insulator, so charge stays; metal conducts it to earth
05-static-electricity.explain: Insulators trap transferred charge in place. On earthed metal, electrons flow through the conductor to earth, so no charge accumulates — the 2025 Q2 answer.

05-static-electricity.q: What is the name of the laboratory instrument that detects charge?
05-static-electricity.explain: The gold-leaf electroscope — named in the specification, and the examiners deduct the mark if it cannot be named.

05-static-electricity.q: In a gold-leaf electroscope, why does the leaf rise?
options: It is attracted to the case
Leaf and stem gain the same charge and repel
05-static-electricity.explain: Charge spreads over stem and leaf; like charges repel, so the leaf lifts away from the stem.

05-static-electricity.q: Why is refuelling an aircraft a static hazard?
options: Friction between fuel and pipe builds charge that could spark and ignite vapour
05-static-electricity.explain: Fuel flowing through the pipe transfers electrons; charge builds until a spark can jump — which could ignite the fuel vapour.

05-static-electricity.q: How is the refuelling danger reduced?
options: Earthing/bonding the aircraft so charge flows to earth
05-static-electricity.explain: A bonding wire lets electrons flow to earth so charge never accumulates. The mark needs the charge to actually go to earth — 'it's earthed' alone scores nothing.

05-static-electricity.q: Which statement about earthing is complete enough to score?
options: The can is connected to the ground
Electrons flow through the wire to earth, so charge cannot build up
05-static-electricity.explain: Say where the electrons go. Restating that it is earthed simply repeats the question.

05-static-electricity.q: A charged balloon sticks to a wall. Why?
options: It induces an opposite charge on the wall's surface, causing attraction
05-static-electricity.explain: Induced opposite charge on the wall surface attracts the balloon — same induction idea as the paper scraps.

05-static-electricity.q: Which is a genuine use of static electricity?
05-static-electricity.explain: Charged paint droplets repel each other (even coat) and are attracted to the earthed object. Also: photocopiers, precipitators in chimneys.

05-static-electricity.q: In electrostatic paint spraying, why is the car body earthed or oppositely charged?
options: So the charged paint is attracted to it, reducing waste
05-static-electricity.explain: The attraction pulls droplets onto all surfaces, including the back — even coverage, less wasted paint.

05-static-electricity.q: Why do the paint droplets spread into an even cloud?
options: They all carry the same charge and repel
They are attracted to each other
05-static-electricity.explain: Like charges repel — same-charged droplets spread apart into a fine, even mist.

05-static-electricity.q: Which materials are good electrical insulators?
05-static-electricity.explain: Plastic, rubber, glass — electrons cannot flow through them, which is why friction charges them.

05-static-electricity.q: Why can you get a small shock touching a car door after a journey?
options: Friction charged the car (or you); touching lets charge flow suddenly
05-static-electricity.explain: Friction with the seat/air builds charge; on contact the charge flows to earth through you — a tiny spark.

05-static-electricity.q: A charge of 4.5 × 10⁻⁷ C builds up over 90 s. What is the mean current? (Q = I × t)
05-static-electricity.explain: I = Q ÷ t = 4.5 × 10⁻⁷ ÷ 90 = 5.0 × 10⁻⁹ A. Use standard form — the examiners asked for it explicitly.

05-static-electricity.q: Lightning is caused by…
options: Charge separation in clouds discharging as a giant spark
05-static-electricity.explain: Friction between ice/water particles separates charge in the cloud; the buildup discharges as lightning.

05-static-electricity.q: Why are fuel tankers fitted with a bonding wire before loading?
options: To carry static charge safely to earth
05-static-electricity.explain: Same principle as aircraft refuelling — the wire gives electrons a safe path to earth so no spark forms near fuel vapour.

05-static-electricity.q: An acetate rod becomes positively charged when rubbed. What happened?
options: It lost electrons to the cloth
05-static-electricity.explain: Positive charge means electrons were lost. Protons never move.

05-static-electricity.q: The unit of electric charge is the…
05-static-electricity.explain: Charge is measured in coulombs (C).

05-static-electricity.q: A charged rod is brought near a thin stream of water, which bends towards it. Why?
options: The rod induces opposite charge in the near side of the stream
05-static-electricity.explain: Induction again: the near side of the stream becomes oppositely charged and is attracted. (The water itself is not charged — a misconception the 2025 examiners flagged.)

05-static-electricity.q: Which test PROVES an object is charged (rather than just conducting)?
options: It repels an object with the same known charge
05-static-electricity.explain: Attraction can be induction; only repulsion proves like charge. In demonstrations, attraction of an uncharged insulator is accepted as showing charge is present.

05-static-electricity.q: Two students shuffle across a nylon carpet. One touches a radiator and gets a shock. The radiator acts as…
05-static-electricity.explain: The earthed metal radiator gives the accumulated charge a path to earth — hence the sudden discharge.

05-static-electricity.q: Why is it dangerous to fill a plastic fuel can while it sits on a plastic truck bed liner?
options: Nothing conducts the charge away, so a spark can ignite vapour
05-static-electricity.explain: Insulator on insulator: charge from the flowing fuel has nowhere to go. Standard practice is to fill cans on the ground (earthed).

05-static-electricity.q: Which particle diagram shows a NEGATIVE ion?
05-static-electricity.explain: Extra electrons = net negative charge. (Equal numbers = neutral atom.)

05-static-electricity.q: Rubbing transfers 2 × 10¹⁰ electrons to a rod. What can you say about the cloth?
options: It gained the same number of electrons
It lost 2 × 10¹⁰ electrons and is positive
05-static-electricity.explain: Charge is conserved — the electrons the rod gained are exactly the electrons the cloth lost.

05-static-electricity.q: In an electrostatic precipitator (chimney smoke remover), the smoke particles are…
options: Charged, then attracted to earthed/oppositely charged plates
05-static-electricity.explain: Charged smoke particles are attracted to collection plates — static used to clean emissions.

05-static-electricity.q: Why does a TV screen gather dust quickly?
options: The charged screen attracts dust particles
05-static-electricity.explain: The screen's static charge attracts light dust particles — everyday induction.

05-static-electricity.q: A material becomes positively charged when it…
05-static-electricity.explain: Only electrons move. Positive means electrons have been REMOVED — protons are locked in the nucleus and never transfer.

05-static-electricity.q: Two objects are rubbed together. One gains a charge of −5 × 10⁻⁹ C. The other has…
05-static-electricity.explain: Charge is conserved: every electron gained by one was lost by the other, so the charges are equal and opposite.

05-static-electricity.q: A charged rod is held near a thin stream of uncharged water. The stream…
options: is attracted, whichever sign the rod carries
is attracted only if the rod is positive
05-static-electricity.explain: The rod INDUCES an opposite charge on the near side, so the attraction always wins. The examiner's note: any suggestion the water is charged or repelled loses marks.

05-static-electricity.q: Earthing a charged object works because…
options: electrons flow to or from earth through a conductor
05-static-electricity.explain: It provides a conducting path for electrons. Saying only 'it is earthed so it is safe' scores nothing — you must say where the electrons go.

05-static-electricity.q: Why can a metal rod held in your hand not be charged by rubbing?
options: The charge flows through you to earth
Friction does not work on metals
05-static-electricity.explain: Friction transfers electrons in both cases; the metal is a conductor, so the charge immediately drains away through your body to earth. Hold it with an insulating handle and it charges fine.

05-static-electricity.q: The instrument used to detect charge, with a thin metal leaf, is called a…
05-static-electricity.explain: Gold-leaf electroscope — the report notes a mark was deducted for not knowing the name, since it is named in the specification.

05-static-electricity.q: The leaf of an electroscope rises when it is charged because…
options: the leaf and stem carry the same charge and repel
the leaf is attracted to the case
05-static-electricity.explain: Like charges repel: charge spreads over the metal stem and leaf, so they push apart.

05-static-electricity.q: The danger when refuelling an aircraft is that…
options: the fuel becomes charged and explodes on its own
a spark from static charge could ignite the fuel vapour
static electricity makes the metal magnetic
05-static-electricity.explain: Friction charges the pipe and aircraft; a spark acts as an ignition source in a flammable vapour. Prevention: a bonding/earthing wire so electrons flow to earth.

05-static-electricity.q: In electrostatic spray painting, the paint droplets and the object are given…
05-static-electricity.explain: Opposite charges attract, so the paint is pulled evenly onto the object and wraps around it, wasting less. In a photocopier the toner is likewise attracted to oppositely charged areas.

05-static-electricity.q: A charge of 6.0 × 10⁻⁸ C flows in 15 s. The current is…
05-static-electricity.explain: I = Q ÷ t = 6.0 × 10⁻⁸ ÷ 15 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁹ A. The report begged for standard form here and flagged 'far too many POT errors'.

06-radioactivity.q: What is an alpha particle made of?
06-radioactivity.explain: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus: 2 protons + 2 neutrons, charge +2.

06-radioactivity.q: What is a beta particle?
options: A fast-moving electron from the nucleus
06-radioactivity.explain: Beta is a fast electron emitted when a neutron in the nucleus turns into a proton and an electron.

06-radioactivity.q: What is gamma radiation?
06-radioactivity.explain: Gamma is an EM wave — energy, not particles. Mass and charge: both zero.

06-radioactivity.q: Which radiation is the most strongly ionising?
06-radioactivity.explain: Alpha: large, doubly charged, slow — it collides and ionises heavily, which is also why it penetrates least.

06-radioactivity.q: Which radiation is stopped by a few centimetres of air or a sheet of paper?
06-radioactivity.explain: Alpha is absorbed by paper, skin or a few cm of air. Beta needs a few mm of aluminium; gamma needs thick lead or concrete.

06-radioactivity.q: Which radiation passes through paper but is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium?
06-radioactivity.explain: That is the beta signature. It is the standard absorber-identification question.

06-radioactivity.q: In alpha decay, what happens to the mass number and atomic number?
06-radioactivity.explain: The nucleus loses 2 protons + 2 neutrons: mass number down 4, atomic number down 2.

06-radioactivity.q: In beta decay, what happens to the mass number and atomic number?
06-radioactivity.explain: A neutron becomes a proton + electron: mass number unchanged, atomic number up 1.

06-radioactivity.q: Carbon-14 (¹⁴₆C) undergoes beta decay. What does it become?
06-radioactivity.explain: Beta: mass stays 14, atomic number 6 → 7, giving nitrogen-14.

06-radioactivity.q: After gamma emission, the nucleus has…
options: The same mass number and atomic number
06-radioactivity.explain: Gamma carries away energy only — no particles, so the numbers are unchanged.

06-radioactivity.q: What is the half-life of a radioactive substance?
options: Half the time it stays radioactive
The time for a nucleus to halve
The time for the activity of a sample to halve
06-radioactivity.explain: The time for the activity (or number of undecayed nuclei) of a SAMPLE to halve. 'A nucleus halving' scores zero — a specific examiner ruling.

06-radioactivity.q: A source's activity is 800 Bq with half-life 6 days. What is the activity after 24 days?
A tracer has activity 12 000 Bq and half-life 6 hours. What is the activity after one day?
What is the unit of radioactive activity?
06-radioactivity.explain: Activity — decays per second — is measured in becquerel (Bq).

06-radioactivity.q: What is background radiation?
options: Ionising radiation that is present at all times, from sources around us
06-radioactivity.explain: It is always present. Don't use the word 'background' in the definition, and don't claim it is only natural — both penalised in 2025.

06-radioactivity.q: Which is a named source of background radiation?
06-radioactivity.explain: Accepted sources: rocks/soil (radon), cosmic rays, food, medical equipment, weapons testing. 'Stars' was rejected.

06-radioactivity.q: Radioactive decay is described as random. What does that mean?
options: You cannot predict when a particular nucleus will decay
The radiation goes in random colours
06-radioactivity.explain: No way to predict which nucleus decays next or when — only the statistical behaviour (half-life) of large numbers is predictable.

06-radioactivity.q: Why is gamma used for medical tracers rather than alpha?
options: Gamma penetrates out of the body to be detected; alpha would be absorbed and cause damage inside
06-radioactivity.explain: Gamma escapes the body to reach the detector; alpha would be stopped within centimetres of tissue and, being heavily ionising, damage cells.

06-radioactivity.q: What is the difference between contamination and irradiation?
options: Contamination: radioactive material gets onto/into the object. Irradiation: exposure to radiation from outside
06-radioactivity.explain: Contaminated objects carry the source with them; irradiated objects were exposed but are not radioactive afterwards.

06-radioactivity.q: Which use suits alpha's properties?
06-radioactivity.explain: Alpha ionises the air gap in a smoke detector; smoke disrupts the tiny current. Its short range makes it safe in the home.

06-radioactivity.q: Which radiation suits monitoring the thickness of aluminium foil in a factory?
06-radioactivity.explain: Beta is partially absorbed by thin metal — thickness changes show as count-rate changes. Alpha would all stop; gamma would all pass.

06-radioactivity.q: What is nuclear fission?
options: A large nucleus splitting into smaller nuclei, releasing energy
06-radioactivity.explain: Fission: a heavy nucleus (e.g. uranium-235) splits, releasing energy and neutrons that can sustain a chain reaction.

06-radioactivity.q: What is nuclear fusion?
options: Light nuclei joining to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy
06-radioactivity.explain: Fusion: light nuclei (hydrogen) join — the process powering the Sun and other stars.

06-radioactivity.q: Where does fusion happen naturally?
06-radioactivity.explain: Stars fuse hydrogen into helium. Fission is what current nuclear power stations use.

06-radioactivity.q: The atomic (proton) number of a nucleus is…
06-radioactivity.explain: Atomic number = protons (which defines the element). Mass number = protons + neutrons.

06-radioactivity.q: Isotopes of an element have…
06-radioactivity.explain: Same element (same protons), different neutron count — so different mass numbers.

06-radioactivity.q: ²³⁸₉₂U emits an alpha particle. What is the product?
06-radioactivity.explain: Mass 238 − 4 = 234; atomic 92 − 2 = 90 → thorium-234.

06-radioactivity.q: Why must school radioactive sources be handled with tongs?
options: Distance greatly reduces the radiation dose received
06-radioactivity.explain: Dose falls sharply with distance; tongs, short exposure time and pointing away are the standard precautions.

06-radioactivity.q: A Geiger counter reads 30 counts/min with no source present. What is this reading?
06-radioactivity.explain: That is background count. Subtract it from measurements before calculating half-life from readings.

06-radioactivity.q: A count rate falls from 600 to 300 counts/s in 19 minutes. What is the half-life?
06-radioactivity.explain: Halving from 600 to 300 took 19 minutes — that is one half-life. Read it straight from a graph the same way.

06-radioactivity.q: Which statement about gamma emission is correct?
options: The nucleus loses energy, not particles
06-radioactivity.explain: Gamma is pure energy — the nucleus de-excites, no change to mass or atomic number.

06-radioactivity.q: An ion is formed when an atom…
06-radioactivity.explain: Ionisation is the removal (or gain) of electrons — which is exactly the damage ionising radiation does to atoms in cells.

06-radioactivity.q: An alpha particle consists of…
06-radioactivity.explain: A helium nucleus: 2 protons + 2 neutrons. Beta is a fast electron from the nucleus; gamma is an EM wave carrying no mass or charge.

06-radioactivity.q: Which radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper?
06-radioactivity.explain: Alpha: paper or a few cm of air. Beta: a few mm of aluminium. Gamma: only reduced by thick lead or concrete — never fully stopped.

06-radioactivity.q: Which radiation is the most strongly ionising?
06-radioactivity.explain: Alpha ionises most (and so penetrates least — the two go together). It is the most dangerous INSIDE the body for exactly that reason.

06-radioactivity.q: During alpha decay the mass number and atomic number change by…
06-radioactivity.explain: Losing 2 protons and 2 neutrons: mass −4, atomic −2. Beta decay: mass unchanged, atomic +1. Gamma: both unchanged.

06-radioactivity.q: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time for…
options: half the undecayed nuclei to decay
06-radioactivity.explain: Half the remaining unstable nuclei decay (equivalently, the activity halves). It is constant for a given isotope and unaffected by temperature or chemistry.

06-radioactivity.q: A sample has an activity of 800 Bq and a half-life of 2 hours. After 6 hours the activity is…
06-radioactivity.explain: 6 hours = three half-lives: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100 Bq. Count the halvings; the activity never reaches exactly zero.

06-radioactivity.q: Background radiation comes mainly from…
options: natural sources such as rocks, cosmic rays and food
06-radioactivity.explain: Mostly natural — radon gas from rocks, cosmic rays, food and building materials. Background must be SUBTRACTED from readings before analysing a source.

06-radioactivity.q: In beta decay, the particle emitted comes from…
options: a neutron in the nucleus changing into a proton
06-radioactivity.explain: A neutron becomes a proton plus a fast electron (the beta particle), which is why the atomic number rises by one while the mass number stays the same.

06-radioactivity.q: Which is the safest way to handle a radioactive source in the school lab?
options: Hold it in your bare hand briefly
Use long tongs, keep it at arm's length and point it away from people
06-radioactivity.explain: Maximise distance, minimise time, use shielding and handling tools, store it in a lead-lined container.

06-radioactivity.q: An isotope used to check for leaks in an underground pipe should be…
options: an alpha emitter with a long half-life
a gamma emitter with a short half-life
an alpha emitter with a short half-life
a gamma emitter with a half-life of thousands of years
06-radioactivity.explain: Gamma penetrates the soil to be detected at the surface; a short half-life means it does not linger in the environment. Matching radiation type and half-life to the JOB is the standard exam reasoning.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: In an investigation, what is the independent variable?
options: The one you keep the same
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Independent: you change it. Dependent: you measure it. Control: you keep it the same.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: What is the dependent variable?
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: The dependent variable responds to your changes and is what you measure. It goes on the y-axis.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: A student investigates how spring extension varies with force. What is the independent variable?
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Force is deliberately changed; extension is measured (dependent); same spring throughout (control).

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: What makes an investigation VALID?
options: Controlling all variables except the one under test
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Validity = a fair test: only the independent variable changes. Reliability is about repeats and consistency — they are different questions.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: What makes results RELIABLE?
options: Repeating measurements and getting consistent values, taking a mean
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Reliability = repeats + consistency. 'Repeat each measurement three times and calculate a mean' is the accepted wording.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: Which phrase is TOO VAGUE to earn the reliability mark?
options: Repeat each measurement three times and calculate a mean
Repeat at each force and average
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: 'Repeat the experiment' and 'take more readings' are on the examiners' list of phrases that score nothing — say what is repeated and what you do with the repeats.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: When should you use a line graph rather than a bar chart?
options: When you have lots of data
When the data is in categories
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Continuous vs continuous → line graph. Categoric data (e.g. type of metal) → bar chart. The word 'continuous' is what the mark scheme wants.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: A student compares four different metals. Which graph type is right?
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Metal type is categoric (discrete) data — a bar chart. The 2025 examiner 'held out specifically for the right vocab': categoric or discrete.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: One point lies far off the trend of the others. What should the student do?
options: Include it in the line of best fit
Repeat that measurement and exclude it from the line if it cannot be reproduced
Move the point onto the line
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Identify the anomaly, repeat that reading, and leave it out of the best-fit line if it is not reproducible.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: What is the best way to plot data points on graph paper?
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: The examiners: papers get scanned — plot with a clear X, not dots 'so small I couldn't actually see all of them'.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: What must every graph axis carry?
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Label each axis with the quantity AND its unit (e.g. 'Force in N'). Missing units is a standard lost mark.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: What makes a graph scale 'sensible'?
options: The data fills at least half the grid and every point is easy to plot
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Use at least half the grid, pick easy multiples. The examiners explicitly reject scales based on 30s ('multiples of 30, 45, 60, 80').

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: A line of best fit should…
options: Pass smoothly through the trend, balancing points either side, ignoring anomalies
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Smooth line (straight OR curved) following the trend, ignoring anomalies. Dot-to-dot lines lose the mark.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: When should a line of best fit be a curve?
options: When the points clearly follow a curved trend
When you have fewer than 5 points
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Fit the trend the data shows. Forcing a straight line through curved data (like an I–V filament graph) is wrong.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: Why include (0,0) as a data point when appropriate?
options: If the theory says zero input gives zero output, it is a genuine data point
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: When zero force gives zero extension (etc.), the origin is a real, free data point — include it.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: In the spring investigation, which is the correct control variable?
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Control what could otherwise change the outcome: same spring, same temperature, ruler vertical.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: How is the extension of a spring calculated?
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Extension = stretched length − natural length. Recording total length instead of extension is a classic error.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: How should a student avoid parallax error when reading a ruler?
options: Read at eye level, straight on
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Read with the eye level with the marker. Parallax = apparent shift from reading at an angle.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: The examiners' accepted improvement instead of 'be more accurate' is…
options: Use a measuring instrument with a finer resolution
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Name the improvement: an instrument with finer resolution (micrometer instead of ruler). Vague 'more accurate' scores nothing.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: A student measures each extension once with one spring per force. Give a criticism.
options: No repeats, and different springs change more than one variable
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Two flaws the diagnostic asks for: no repeats (unreliable) and different springs (invalid — not a fair test).

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: What does the resolution of an instrument mean?
options: The smallest change it can detect
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Resolution = smallest division/detectable change, e.g. 1 mm on a ruler, 0.01 mm on a micrometer.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: Which is the correct order for describing a method?
options: What to change, what to measure, what to control, repeats
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: The eight-point skeleton: variables (change/measure/control), equipment, procedure, range, repeats, and how results will be used.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: A results table should show…
options: All repeats plus the calculated mean, with units in the headers
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Show repeats and means; units live in the column headers, not next to every number.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: A student's five repeats: 2.1, 2.0, 2.2, 4.8, 2.1. What is the correct mean?
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: 4.8 is an anomaly — exclude it. Mean of the rest = (2.1+2.0+2.2+2.1) ÷ 4 = 2.1.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: What is a range in an investigation?
options: The spread of independent-variable values tested (e.g. 1 N to 6 N)
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Range = the span of values of the independent variable. 'Take readings across a wider range' is the accepted improvement wording.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: Why take readings at more values of the independent variable (not just repeats)?
options: To see the shape of the relationship more clearly
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: More values across the range reveal the trend (straight vs curved). Repeats address reliability; more values address the trend.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: In 'how does temperature affect thermistor resistance', the water bath temperature is the…
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Temperature is deliberately changed → independent. Resistance is measured → dependent.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: The 2023 examiner rejected 'same size or volume' as a control for rods. What was wanted?
options: Same length and same diameter, named separately
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Name the dimensions specifically — length, diameter/thickness. 'Size' and 'volume' were judged too loose.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: An improvement question asks 'what can be done to improve the method'. Which answer style scores?
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Say what to DO — 'use rods of the same length' — not just 'the rods weren't the same length'. Students lost marks for exactly this in 2025.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: Which pairing is correct?
options: Validity–fair test and controlled variables; reliability–repeats and consistency
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Validity = fair test (control variables). Reliability = repeats and consistency. They are asked as separate questions — keep them separate.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: The variable you deliberately change in an experiment is the…
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Independent = what you change; dependent = what you measure; control = what you keep the same to make the test valid.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: A set of repeat readings is very close together but all far from the true value. The results are…
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Precise = tightly grouped; accurate = close to the true value. This pattern signals a systematic error, such as a zero error on the instrument.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: An anomalous result should be…
options: identified and excluded from the mean
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Identify it, leave it visible in the table, but exclude it from the mean — and ignore it when drawing a line of best fit.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: "Repeat the experiment" is too vague. A better answer is…
options: repeat each measurement three times and calculate a mean
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Say how many repeats and what you do with them. The department's list of thrown-away marks names this exact vagueness.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: To improve resolution when measuring the diameter of a wire, you should use…
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: A micrometer resolves to 0.01 mm. 'Be more accurate' scores nothing — name the instrument and why it is better.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: The mean of 4.2, 4.4, 4.3 and an anomaly of 7.9 is best given as…
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Discard the anomaly first: (4.2 + 4.4 + 4.3) ÷ 3 = 4.3. Including it drags the mean to a value no reading supports.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: On a graph, the independent variable goes on the…
options: the axis with the larger numbers
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Independent on x (horizontal), dependent on y. Both axes need a quantity AND a unit — a labelling mark on nearly every graph question.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: A line of best fit should…
options: show the trend with points evenly spread either side
be drawn freehand through the last point
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: A single smooth line showing the trend, ignoring anomalies, with roughly equal numbers of points on each side. It only goes through the origin if the data says so.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: Which is a correct unit for density?
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Mass ÷ volume → kg/m³ (or g/cm³). N/kg is gravitational field strength; m³/kg is density upside down.

07-practical-and-data-skills.q: The result 0.04725 m given to 3 significant figures is…
07-practical-and-data-skills.explain: Leading zeros do not count as significant figures: the digits are 4, 7, 2 → round to 0.0473. Answers should be given to the same precision as the data.

08-energy.q: What does the principle of conservation of energy state?
options: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores
08-energy.explain: Energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred, stored or dissipated.

08-energy.q: A ball is held above the ground. Which energy store is filled?
08-energy.explain: Raised objects store gravitational potential energy.

08-energy.q: A stretched rubber band stores energy in which store?
08-energy.explain: Stretched or squashed objects fill the elastic store — the 2025 paper's exact question.

08-energy.q: A falling ball transfers energy from which store to which?
08-energy.explain: Falling: gravitational potential store empties into the kinetic store.

08-energy.q: By which pathway is energy transferred when a person stretches a band?
08-energy.explain: A force moving through a distance transfers energy mechanically — 'by working'.

08-energy.q: What is the correct equation for efficiency?
08-energy.explain: Efficiency = useful energy OUTPUT ÷ total energy INPUT. Omitting 'output' or 'input' loses the mark — the examiners refuse 'useful energy over total energy'.

08-energy.q: A motor receives 800 J and does 240 J of useful work. What is its efficiency?
A machine is 15% efficient with 165 J input. How much energy is WASTED?
08-energy.explain: Useful = 0.15 × 165 ≈ 25 J; wasted = 165 − 25 = 140 J — the 2023 calculation.

08-energy.q: In a Sankey diagram, what does the width of each arrow represent?
08-energy.explain: Arrow width is proportional to energy. The examiners judge the scale by eye — widths must be roughly right and sum to the input width.

08-energy.q: In a Sankey diagram, how must the wasted energy arrow be labelled?
08-energy.explain: The wasted arrow must say thermal/heat — 'transferred to surroundings' alone was refused in 2023.

08-energy.q: Which equation links work done, force and distance?
08-energy.explain: Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force.

08-energy.q: A crane lifts a 3.0 kg mass through 2.5 m (g = 10 N/kg). What GPE is gained?
What is the kinetic energy of a 2 kg ball moving at 3 m/s?
08-energy.explain: KE = ½ × m × v² = ½ × 2 × 9 = 9 J.

08-energy.q: A car doubles its speed. Its kinetic energy…
08-energy.explain: KE depends on v² — doubling speed quadruples the kinetic energy (the same square law as braking distance).

08-energy.q: 45 J of work moves a toy car 7.5 m. What average force acted?
08-energy.explain: F = W ÷ d = 45 ÷ 7.5 = 6.0 N — the 2023 calculation, where many multiplied instead of dividing.

08-energy.q: Which equation links power, work done and time?
08-energy.explain: Power = work done ÷ time taken. One watt is one joule per second.

08-energy.q: A motor does 1200 J of work in 60 s. What is its power?
A ball falls at constant (terminal) velocity. What happens to the GPE it loses?
options: It is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings by air resistance
08-energy.explain: Speed constant → KE constant. All the lost GPE is dissipated thermally by air resistance — the mock's exact reasoning.

08-energy.q: Why is the KE of a dropped ball just before landing less than the GPE it started with?
options: Some energy transferred to the thermal store via air resistance
08-energy.explain: Conservation holds — the difference went to the surroundings as thermal energy via air resistance.

08-energy.q: Which phrase should replace 'energy is lost' in an exam answer?
options: Energy is dissipated to the surroundings
08-energy.explain: Dissipated / transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings. 'Lost' invites the examiner to think you believe energy is destroyed.

08-energy.q: A pendulum swings. At the lowest point of its swing it has maximum…
08-energy.explain: Lowest point: minimum height (GPE) and maximum speed (KE). The stores trade back and forth each swing.

08-energy.q: Using mgh = ½mv², from what height must an object fall (g = 10) to reach 13 m/s? (2 s.f.)
08-energy.explain: h = v² ÷ 2g = 169 ÷ 20 = 8.45 → 8.5 m to 2 s.f. In 2025, 'a significant number' gave 8.45 (2 d.p.) instead of 2 s.f. and lost the mark.

08-energy.q: Which energy resource is non-renewable?
08-energy.explain: Fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) are non-renewable. Wind, solar, hydro, tidal, geothermal and biomass are renewable.

08-energy.q: In a fossil-fuel power station, the correct energy sequence is…
08-energy.explain: Fuel burns (chemical → thermal), steam turns turbine (thermal → kinetic), generator (kinetic → electrical).

08-energy.q: Which pathway transfers energy from the Sun to Earth?
08-energy.explain: Space is a vacuum — only radiation (EM waves) crosses it.

08-energy.q: A 60 kg runner moves at 8 m/s. What is their kinetic energy?
08-energy.explain: KE = ½ × 60 × 8² = ½ × 60 × 64 = 1920 J. Square the speed first.

08-energy.q: The main way to reduce unwanted thermal transfer from a house roof is…
08-energy.explain: Insulation traps air — a poor conductor — reducing transfer by conduction and convection.

08-energy.q: Which store fills when a fuel burns?
options: The thermal store of the surroundings increases
08-energy.explain: Burning empties the fuel's chemical store into thermal stores. (In the 2024 MCQ, 'chemical store increases' was the trap — burning decreases it.)

08-energy.q: 2.2 kW in watts is…
08-energy.explain: kilo = ×1000: 2.2 kW = 2200 W — a one-mark conversion from the 2024 paper.

08-energy.q: How many seconds are in one hour?
08-energy.explain: 60 × 60 = 3600 s. (86 400 is a day — the 2024 distractor.)

08-energy.q: In an efficiency calculation the answer comes out as 1.4. What does this tell you?
options: You have made an error — efficiency cannot exceed 1 (100%)
The units are wrong but the answer right
08-energy.explain: Efficiency above 1 would mean creating energy — impossible. It usually means output and input were swapped in the fraction.

08-energy.q: A Sankey diagram shows 100 J in, 40 J useful out. How much is dissipated, and how wide should its arrow be relative to the useful arrow?
08-energy.explain: Dissipated = 100 − 40 = 60 J; arrows scale with energy, so 60 J is 1.5× the width of the 40 J arrow.

08-energy.q: The law of conservation of energy states that energy…
options: is used up when work is done
cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred
08-energy.explain: Transferred between stores, never created or destroyed. 'Energy is lost' means transferred to a less useful store (usually thermal), not destroyed.

08-energy.q: Work done is calculated as…
